review_notes: I read the whole file and did not open any other sources. I looked for repeated reasoning that is both nontrivial and shared between at least two proofs. The parallel families are Periodic/Antiperiodic (`const_add`, `add_const`, `const_sub`, `sub_const`, `const_smul`, `const_inv_smul`, `neg`, `sub_eq`), the nsmul/zsmul/nat_mul/int_mul variants, and `map_vadd_zmultiples`/`map_vadd_multiples`. Each of these proofs is one to three lines. Most are `simpa only [...]` calls, small `rw` chains, or direct uses of the previous lemma. They repeat routine unfolding and rewriting, not substantial reasoning. A shared lemma would also have to be generic over `Periodic` versus `Antiperiodic`, or over the additive structure. That would add statement overhead and would not remove any real proof complexity. The longest parallel pair is `add_zsmul_eq` and `add_nsmul_eq`, which both split on parity and apply the even/odd lemmas. The two instances differ in the `Int` versus `Nat` API they use (`negOnePow`, units, `zsmul` versus `pow`, `simp`). Factoring them would be a wrapper-style change or would move branches into a helper, and the rubric rules both out. I found no justified finding.
